doc.title: Buster Williams interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: Apprenticeship, Milt Hinton and why the winner finishes last
summary: He argues young musicians are pushed away from apprenticeship, citing Milt Hinton's late recognition and the story of the big bull and little bull.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well you said you had an apprenticeship of about 30 years before you put your band together. As you said, it’s quite different these days with — it seems like the young musicians get pushed into that role.
They get pushed away from where they need to be in order to establish something that’s long-going. In this business the winner is the one who finishes last.

Well let’s look at it. Look at Milt Hinton. Milt Hinton and I were on a movie date we were doing for Spike Lee, called “Clockers.” Now I’ve known Milt for a long time. And Milt was, this was about six or seven years ago. So he was already up in years. And he had just done his first record as a leader. All these years, I mean playing with everybody, you know, Milton Berle, Bing Crosby, you know, and we were talking one day during the break and we were talking about all the attention that he was getting now. He says, “Where was everybody when I needed them? I could have used this thirty years ago.” But that’s what I’m talking about. Finishing. I mean you stay around long enough and it’s all going to come to you just by virtue of the fact that you’re still here. “What, you’re still here?” © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

You know, you deserve — so I mean hopefully things change to the point where it doesn’t get to that. I feel that people need to be honored while they’re alive. If they’re worth anything while they’re dead they must be worth something while they’re alive. So that’s what I mean by the winner is the one who finishes last. The one who stays around. I mean even in this society, a society such as the Asian society and Japan, they know how to treat elderly people. When people become old, they don’t throw them aside. There’s a wisdom that they have now. There’s an intelligence that they have now. There’s a wealth of experience that they have now that others can benefit from. You know the story of the bull? The big bull and the little bull? Up on top of the hill? And they’re looking down into the valley and all of these cows are down there grazing you know? And the little bull is all excited, and he’s feeling his oats, and he looks at the big bull and he says, “Why don’t we run down there and make love to one of those cows?” And the big bull looks at the little bull chewing his cud and he says, “Why don’t we walk down there and make love to all of them?” You know? You only get that wisdom from experience. You’ve got to live a little bit.
